candidates.quote: Do any human beings ever realize life while they live it?—every, every minute?
candidates.author: Thornton Wilder
candidates.speaker: Emily Webb
candidates.whyThisMonth: The question the whole play is built to ask, and a reader can answer it by looking up from the page at the room around them.

candidates.quote: There is always something left to love.
candidates.author: Lorraine Hansberry
candidates.speaker: Lena Younger (Mama), to Beneatha
candidates.whyThisMonth: Beneatha has just said there is nothing left to love, and Mama names the one thing that does not pass: the month's other half, stated in seven words.

candidates.quote: Let us do something, while we have the chance!
candidates.author: Samuel Beckett
candidates.speaker: Vladimir
candidates.whyThisMonth: Two men with nothing coming still decide to act, and the whole force of it is in the clause about the chance.

candidates.quote: I didn’t go to the moon, I went much further—for time is the longest distance between two places.
candidates.author: Tennessee Williams
candidates.locator: scene seven, the closing speech (New Directions, 1945)
candidates.speaker: Tom Wingfield
candidates.whyThisMonth: Tom has crossed a continent and learned that the distance that counts is measured in years, which is the quiet fact of the month: editions differ on whether the dash is spaced.

candidates.quote: See how deepest purple, brightest scarlet / open their beauty only to dry well crumbling.
candidates.author: Tang Xianzu
candidates.locator: scene 10, The Interrupted Dream, p. 44 (2nd ed., Indiana University Press, 2002)
candidates.speaker: Bridal Du (Du Liniang)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The garden aria the play is known by names beauty and ruin in one breath, so a morning reader is not asked to choose between them.

candidates.quote: Nothing beside remains. Round the decay / Of that colossal wreck, boundless and bare / The lone and level sands stretch far away.
candidates.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
candidates.locator: lines 12 to 14 (first printed in The Examiner, 11 January 1818)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The boast is gone and the sand is still there, the theme stated once and for all without a word of gloom: modern editions print colossal wreck in lower case where the 1818 printing capitalises Wreck.

candidates.quote: Better by far you should forget and smile / Than that you should remember and be sad.
candidates.author: Christina Rossetti
candidates.locator: lines 13 to 14, the closing couplet, Goblin Market and Other Poems (Macmillan, 1862)
candidates.whyThisMonth: She releases the person she is leaving, and a reader carries that generosity into a day full of smaller losses.

candidates.quote: The flowers withered, / Their color faded away, / While meaninglessly / I spent my days in the world / And the long rains were falling.
candidates.author: Ono no Komachi
candidates.locator: poem 113, in Anthology of Japanese Literature, p. 78 (Grove Press, 1955)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest warning against spending a life without noticing it, and it arrives before the day has been spent.

candidates.quote: Loveliest of what I have left behind is the sunlight, / And loveliest after that is the shining stars and the moon’s face, / But also cucumbers that are ripe, and pears and apples.
candidates.author: Praxilla
candidates.locator: fragment 747 (Page, Poetae Melici Graeci), in Greek Lyrics (2nd ed., University of Chicago Press, 1960)
candidates.speaker: Adonis
candidates.whyThisMonth: Asked what he misses, Adonis answers sunlight, stars and ripe cucumbers, which is the best argument there is for paying attention at breakfast: the Lattimore wording is confirmed in two independent quotations but no page of Greek Lyrics was sighted.

candidates.quote: All things are changing; nothing dies.
candidates.author: Ovid
candidates.locator: Book XV, line 165, Loeb Classical Library vol. 2 (Heinemann and Putnam, 1916)
candidates.speaker: Pythagoras
candidates.whyThisMonth: Pythagoras states the month's consolation in five words, that change is not loss, and Ovid gives the whole poem to proving it.

candidates.quote: But where are the snows of yester-year?
candidates.author: François Villon
candidates.work: The Ballad of Dead Ladies (Ballade des dames du temps jadis)
candidates.locator: the refrain, in The Complete Poetical Works of Dante Gabriel Rossetti (Roberts Brothers, 1887), pp. 237 to 238
candidates.whyThisMonth: The one question the whole ubi sunt tradition is known by, asked lightly enough that a reader can carry it about all day.

candidates.quote: Though a country be sundered, hills and rivers endure; / And spring comes green again to trees and grasses / Where petals have been shed like tears / And lonely birds have sung their grief.
candidates.author: Du Fu
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 4, The Jade Mountain (Alfred A. Knopf, 1929)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The state falls, the hills stay and the grass comes back, which is precisely what a reader wants told to them at first light.

candidates.quote: Though leaves are many, the root is one; / Through all the lying days of my youth / I swayed my leaves and flowers in the sun; / Now I may wither into the truth.
candidates.author: W. B. Yeats
candidates.work: The Coming of Wisdom with Time
candidates.locator: the whole poem, The Green Helmet and Other Poems (Cuala Press, 1910)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Four lines on what goes and what holds, ending in the only promise this month can honestly make.

candidates.quote: The art of losing isn’t hard to master; / so many things seem filled with the intent / to be lost that their loss is no disaster.
candidates.author: Elizabeth Bishop
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 3, Geography III (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1976)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The villanelle opens by pretending that losing is easy, and the pretence is the kindest possible way into the subject.

candidates.quote: We look at the world once, in childhood. / The rest is memory.
candidates.author: Louise Glück
candidates.whyThisMonth: Two lines that say why memory aches, and say it with no trace of self-pity, which is the tone the month needs.

candidates.quote: But not because of its magnificence / Dear is the Casuarina to my soul: / Beneath it we have played; though years may roll, / O sweet companions, loved with love intense, / For your sakes, shall the tree be ever dear.
candidates.author: Toru Dutt
candidates.locator: stanza 3, Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan (Kegan Paul, Trench and Co., 1882)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The tree is loved for the hours spent under it and not for its grandeur, which is the month's quiet argument for attention.
